summaries.example: Imagine a rainbow. You see a colorful band in the sky, but the rainbow also depends on water drops, light, and where you are standing. Kant uses examples like this to show that an object can be considered as it appears to us and also as it may be independently of our way of sensing it. Science can teach us more about the rainbow, but Kant says that this still tells us about the world as it can appear in experience, not about things completely beyond experience.
summaries.summary: Kant’s transcendental idealism begins with a difference between appearances and things in themselves. An appearance is an object as human beings can experience it through the senses, in space and time. A thing in itself is that object considered independently of our way of experiencing it. Kant argues that we can know appearances, but we cannot know the inner nature of things in themselves. Still, we can think about them. He also separates his view from two other positions. Transcendental realism treats space, time, and objects as existing independently of our experience. Empirical idealism doubts or denies that objects outside the mind can be known. Kant instead says that ordinary objects in space are real as objects of experience, even though they are not known as things in themselves. Readers of Kant have long disagreed about exactly how appearances depend on minds and how they relate to things in themselves.
key_ideas: We experience objects in space and events in time as appearances.
Kant says space and time are forms of human experience, not independent things we can know by themselves.
We can think about things in themselves, but we cannot gain ordinary knowledge of what they are like beyond experience.
Kant’s view is not the same as saying that everyday objects are simply imaginary or illusions.
Philosophers disagree about whether an appearance and a thing in itself are two objects or two ways of considering one object.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kant’s ideas ask us to notice the difference between the world we experience and questions about reality beyond every possible experience. This can help us understand why science gives powerful knowledge while still having limits. It also shows why philosophers carefully distinguish an object, our experience of it, and the conditions that make experience possible.

important_terms.definition: What we experience through our senses, such as objects in space and events in time.
Something considered as it exists independently of how people experience it. Kant says we cannot know its inner nature.
Kant’s view that space and time belong to the way human beings experience things, rather than being known as independent objects.
The ability to take in information through the senses.

questions_to_think_about: Could two people experience the same object differently while still talking about one real object?
What is the difference between thinking about something and knowing it?
If science discovers hidden parts of an object, has it found a thing in itself, or learned more about an appearance?
Why might space and time be part of our way of experiencing things?

summaries.example: Consider a rainbow observed from two locations. Its visible colors depend partly on the observer’s position and sensory organization, while its physical conditions can be studied through water droplets, light, and spatial relations. Kant’s empirical distinction between an object’s more observer-independent physical features and its sensory appearance is not yet the transcendental appearance/thing-in-itself distinction. Even a scientific account of the droplets and light remains an account of objects in space and time—appearances in the transcendental sense, not knowledge of things in themselves.
summaries.summary: Kant’s transcendental idealism concerns the conditions under which human beings experience objects. Space and time are not independent containers or features known to belong to things as they are in themselves. They are forms of sensible intuition: ways in which objects are given to human cognition. Objects encountered in space and time are therefore appearances. This does not mean they are unreal, private images, or doubtful in the ordinary sense. Kant’s position is also a form of empirical realism: we can have immediate knowledge of objects in space through experience, rather than inferring them from inner states. The difficult question is what appearances are and how they relate to things in themselves. Kant says that things in themselves are not cognizable by us, although they can be thought about and are connected in his account with our being affected in experience. The entry surveys competing interpretations. Phenomenalist readings make appearances depend partly or wholly on representations or experience. Dual-aspect readings instead treat the distinction as two standpoints or sets of properties belonging to objects. The text also distinguishes things in themselves from noumena and from the transcendental object, which is the abstract idea of an object in general.
key_ideas: Space and time are not, for Kant, independently known entities or properties of things as they are in themselves; they are forms of human sensible intuition.
Because cognition requires intuition, human beings cognize objects only as appearances in space and time.
Kant denies that transcendental idealism makes bodies mere illusions. He treats objects in space as empirically real and directly knowable in experience.

The ordinary distinction between how an object looks and how it physically is is only an empirical appearance/reality distinction. Scientific discoveries still concern appearances in the transcendental sense.
Kant allows that we can think about things in themselves using general concepts, but such thinking does not amount to cognition of their positive properties.
Interpretations differ: some read Kant as a phenomenalist, while epistemic and metaphysical dual-aspect readings understand the appearance/thing-in-itself distinction in less subjectivist ways.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kant’s view separates questions about what exists independently of human cognition from questions about what makes knowledge possible for beings like us. That distinction influences debates about realism, scientific knowledge, perception, and the limits of metaphysics. The continuing disagreement also teaches an important philosophical lesson: a theory’s central terms may support several interpretations, and understanding a position requires examining how its claims fit together.

important_terms.definition: An object as it is given in possible human experience, structured by the forms of intuition and thought available to us.
An object, or an aspect of an object, considered independently of the conditions of human sensibility; Kant says its positive nature is not cognized by us.
The doctrine that space and time are forms of our sensible intuition, so objects known by us are appearances rather than things known independently of our cognition.
The position that space and time, and objects located in them, exist independently of our sensibility.
The view that we immediately know only our own mental states and can at best infer external objects; Kant distinguishes dogmatic and problematic forms.
The sensory capacity through which objects are given to us; outer sense is ordered spatially and inner sense temporally.
A possible object of a non-sensible, intellectual intuition; in the negative sense, an object not given in our sensible intuition.
The abstract concept of an object in general that helps organize representations into experience, without itself supplying a determinate object.

questions_to_think_about: Does saying that space is a form of intuition make external objects mind-dependent, or only dependent in how they can be known?
Why does Kant distinguish transcendental idealism from empirical idealism?
Can a thing be known scientifically without being known as it is in itself?
Is the appearance/thing-in-itself distinction about two objects, two aspects of one object, or two ways of considering objects?
How might Kant’s claims about things in themselves being unknowable conflict with his claims that they exist or affect us?

summaries.example: Suppose a class watches a rainbow from different places. Students may see slightly different colors or shapes because their viewpoints and senses differ. They can still investigate shared features, such as water drops and light, and build a scientific account. Kant would say that both the colorful view and the scientific account concern appearances in the broad, transcendental sense: objects as they can be experienced and understood in space and time. They do not reveal what the objects are completely apart from every possible way of experiencing them.
summaries.summary: Kant’s transcendental idealism distinguishes objects as they appear in human experience from things in themselves. Space and time are forms of our sensible intuition, meaning that they organize how objects are given to beings with our kind of sensory and intellectual capacities. Since human cognition needs intuition, we can cognize only objects that can in principle appear in space and time. Kant calls these appearances. A thing in itself is considered independently of this mode of access. We can use concepts to think about such things, but we cannot know their positive features as we know an experienced object. Kant insists that this is not empirical idealism: he does not say that external objects are illusions or that their existence is merely doubtful. Objects in space are empirically real and can be known directly in experience. The main interpretive dispute concerns how to understand the dependence of appearances on experience and their relation to things in themselves. A phenomenalist interpretation gives representations a constitutive role in the existence or properties of objects. A dual-aspect interpretation says the distinction may concern different standpoints or different kinds of properties of the same objects. The entry also distinguishes the transcendental issue from ordinary differences between how things look and how they are physically.
key_ideas: Kant says space and time shape how objects are given to human beings; they are not known as things existing independently of sensibility.
We can know appearances because they can be given in experience, but we cannot cognize things in themselves.
Kant’s view does not deny everyday external objects. He calls his position empirically realistic because objects in space are immediately present in experience.
The familiar difference between an object’s appearance to a person and its physical properties is not the same as Kant’s transcendental distinction.
There are several competing interpretations of Kant, including phenomenalist views and dual-aspect views.
Kant’s revisions between the first and second editions of the Critique of Pure Reason led scholars to debate whether his doctrine changed or was mainly presented differently.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate matters because it asks what human knowledge can reach and what it must leave open. Kant’s theory can support confidence in ordinary experience and science while limiting claims about reality beyond possible experience. It also gives students a useful way to compare realism, idealism, and theories that combine elements of both.

important_terms.definition: An object as it is experienced by us through the senses, within space and time.
An object considered independently of our experience. Kant says we may think about it but cannot know its positive nature.
Kant’s position that space and time are forms of our experience, not independent features we can know apart from experience.
The belief that objects in space and time exist independently of our minds and sensibility.
The view that we directly know our own mental states but can only infer whether external objects exist.
Our capacity to receive information through sensation. Outer sense gives spatial experience; inner sense gives awareness of inner states in time.
An object thought as beyond our sensible experience; a positive noumenon would be known by a kind of intellectual intuition that humans do not possess.

questions_to_think_about: If an object is unobserved, does Kant’s theory allow it to continue existing?
Why does Kant think learning more through science still does not give knowledge of things in themselves?
How is empirical idealism different from transcendental idealism?
Could appearances and things in themselves be two perspectives on one object rather than two separate objects?
Why might Kant’s statements about things in themselves affecting us create a philosophical problem?
